{{short description|Class of partial differential equations}}

In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] field of [[differential equation]]s, the '''ultrahyperbolic  equation''' is a class of [[partial differential equation]] (PDE) <ref>{{cite book|author1=Ismael Herrera|author2=George F. Pinder|author2-link=George F. Pinder|chapter-url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1002/9781118207239.app1|title=Mathematical Modeling in Science and Engineering: An Axiomatic Approach.|chapter=APPENDIX A PARTIAL DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS A.1 CLASSIFICATION|publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons, Inc.]] 2012 |quote=In this appendix we study three types of partial differential equations: [[Elliptic partial differential equation|elliptic]], [[Parabolic partial differential equation|parabolic]], and [[Hyperbolic partial differential equation|hyperbolic]] equations. These three classes of equations include the partial differential equations most frequently encountered in engineering and science.}}</ref> first described by [[Richard Courant|R. Courant]]. Specifically non-normal [[Hyperbolic partial differential equation|hyperbolic]]<ref>{{cite book| last1=John | first1=Fritz|author-link=Fritz John|editor=Jürgen Moser|editor-link=Jürgen Moser|chapter-url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.dmj/1077490637|chapter=The ultrahyperbolic differential equation with four independent variables|title=Fritz John Collected Papers Volume 1|edition=1st|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-5406-5 | year=1985 |publisher=[[Birkhäuser]] [[Boston, MA]]: [[Springer Nature]]|issn=0884-7037|quote=Equations which are neither [[Elliptic partial differential equation|elliptic]], nor [[Parabolic partial differential equation|parabolic]], nor normal hyperbolic - have scarcely been treated, at least not without restriction to solutions which are analytic in all or some of the variables. For such equations the notation ''ultrahyperbolic'' has been introduced by R. Courant.}}
</ref> they are used for an unknown [[scalar function]] {{mvar|u}} of {{math|2''n''}} [[Variable (mathematics)|variables]] {{math|''x''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''x''<sub>''n''</sub>, ''y''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''y''<sub>''n''</sub>}} of the form

<math display=block>
\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x_1^2} + \cdots + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x_n^2} - \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y_1^2} - \cdots - \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial y_n^2} = 0.
</math>

More generally, if {{mvar|a}} is any [[quadratic form]] in {{math|2''n''}} variables with [[metric signature|signature]] {{math|(''n'', ''n'')}}, then any PDE whose [[principal part]] is <math>a_{ij}u_{x_ix_j}</math> is said to be ultrahyperbolic.  Any such equation can be put in the form above by means of a change of variables.<ref name="See Courant and Hilbert">See Courant and Hilbert.</ref>

The ultrahyperbolic  equation has been studied from a number of viewpoints.  On the one hand, it resembles the classical [[wave equation]].  This has led to a number of developments concerning its [[Method of characteristics|characteristics]], one of which is due to [[Fritz John]]: the [[John equation]].

In 2008, Walter Craig and Steven Weinstein proved that under a nonlocal constraint, the initial value problem is [[well-posed]] for initial data given on a codimension-one [[hypersurface]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://rspa.royalsocietypublishing.org/content/465/2110/3023 | title = On determinism and well-posedness in multiple time dimensions | publisher = Proc. R. Soc. A vol. 465 no. 2110 3023-3046 (2008) | last1= Craig | first1 = Walter | last2 = Weinstein | first2 = Steven | access-date = 5 December 2013}}</ref> And later, in 2022, a research team at the [[University of Michigan]] extended the conditions for solving ultrahyperbolic wave equations to [[Multiple time dimensions|complex-time]] (kime), demonstrated space-kime dynamics, and showed data science applications using tensor-based linear modeling of [[functional magnetic resonance imaging]] data.<ref>{{cite journal | publisher=Elsevier |author1=Wang, Y |author2= Shen, Y |author3=  Deng, D|author4=  Dinov, ID |date=2022 |title=Determinism, Well-posedness, and Applications of the Ultrahyperbolic Wave Equation in Spacekime |journal=Partial Differential Equations in Applied Mathematics | doi=10.1016/j.padiff.2022.100280 | volume=5 |article-number=100280 |pmid=36159725 |pmc=9494226 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | publisher=Springer |author1= Zhang, R |author2= Zhang, Y |author3=  Liu, Y | author4=  Guo, Y |author5= Shen, Y |author6=  Deng, D |author7= Qiu, Y |author8=  Dinov, ID |date=2022 | title=Kimesurface Representation and Tensor Linear Modeling of Longitudinal Data |journal=Partial Differential Equations in Applied Mathematics | doi=10.1007/s00521-021-06789-8 | volume=34 |issue= 8 |pages=6377–6396|pmid= 35936508 |pmc= 9355340 }}</ref>

The equation has also been studied from the point of view of [[symmetric space]]s, and [[elliptic differential operator]]s.<ref>{{cite journal | publisher=Institut Mittag-Leffler |author1= Helgason, S |date=1959| title=Differential operators on homogeneous spaces |journal=Acta Mathematica | doi=10.1007/BF02564248 | volume=102 | number=3–4 |pages=239–299 | doi-access=free }}</ref>  In particular, the ultrahyperbolic equation satisfies an analog of the [[mean value theorem]] for [[harmonic functions]].
